## 1. Purpose

This SOP establishes the minimum standards for field documentation in
the EA Program. Complete, legible, and contemporaneous field notes are
the foundation of defensible environmental data. Notes recorded in the
field cannot be reconstructed later from memory; what is not written
down at the time is effectively lost. This SOP ensures that every field
visit produces a record sufficient for another trained researcher to
understand what was done, where, when, by whom, and under what
conditions.

For laboratory notebook requirements, see
[SOP-L802 Quality Control](../lab_sops/SOP-L802-quality-control.qmd),
Section 7.1.


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** All EA Program field activities, including sampling,
  sensor deployment/retrieval, site reconnaissance, equipment
  installation, and monitoring visits.
- **Does not apply to:** Laboratory work or purely
  digital data collection on tablets/phones (though digital entries
  should follow the same content standards described here).
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites.


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| Lab PI            | Set documentation standards; review notebooks periodically |
| Field Lead        | Ensure all team members record required entries         |
| All Field Personnel | Maintain a field notebook per this SOP               |
| New Students      | Read this SOP before their first field outing           |


## 4. Notebook Selection and Preparation

### 4.1 Acceptable Notebooks

Use a bound, weather-resistant field notebook with numbered pages. The
following are acceptable:

- Rite in the Rain (top-spiral or side-spiral, any size)
- Any hardbound notebook with numbered pages (if weather protection is
  not needed)

Do **not** use loose-leaf paper, spiral notebooks with perforated pages,
or sticky notes for primary field records.

### 4.2 Front Matter

On the inside front cover or first page of a new notebook, record:

- Your name, phone number, and email
- "If found, please return to: EA Program, Pomona College, SGM 133"
- Project name(s)
- Date the notebook was put into service

### 4.3 Page Numbering

If pages are not pre-numbered, number them in ink before going to the
field. Never remove pages from a field notebook.


## 5. Required Entries for Every Field Visit

Every field visit entry must begin with the following header information.
Write it before you do anything else on site.

### 5.1 Header Block

Record at the top of a new page (or clearly separated section):

| Field               | Example                                       |
|:--------------------|:----------------------------------------------|
| Date                | 2026-05-18 (use ISO format: YYYY-MM-DD)       |
| Time of arrival     | 08:15 PST                                     |
| Site name / ID      | Bernard Field Station, Plot BFS-03             |
| GPS coordinates     | 34.0975 N, 117.7125 W (WGS84)                |
| Personnel present   | M. Los Huertos, J. Smith                       |
| Weather conditions  | Clear, ~25 °C, light wind from W, no recent rain |
| Purpose of visit    | Soil sampling for CN analysis; sensor download |
| SOPs in use         | F56, F61, F72                                  |

### 5.2 Time Stamps

Record the time of every discrete action: sample collection, instrument
reading, equipment start/stop, calibration check, photo taken. Use
24-hour format or AM/PM consistently throughout the notebook.

### 5.3 Site Observations

Before beginning work, take a moment to look around and note anything
relevant:

- Visible changes since the last visit (new construction, vegetation
  removal, standing water, animal activity, vandalism, equipment
  condition)
- Odors or visual indicators of contamination
- Land use activities in progress nearby (mowing, irrigation,
  construction)

### 5.4 Sample and Measurement Records

For each sample collected or measurement taken, record at minimum:

- Sample ID (use the project's naming convention)
- Time of collection/measurement
- Location (plot, transect position, depth, or other descriptor)
- Value or description (e.g., "pH = 7.2," "soil moist, dark brown,
  loamy texture")
- Preservation method applied (e.g., "filtered, acidified with HNO~3~
  to pH <2")
- Container type and label

::: {.callout-tip}
### Write More Than You Think You Need
Include observations that seem obvious at the time. "Soil was saturated
and smelled of sulfide" or "sensor housing had spider web across inlet"
may be critical for interpreting data months later.
:::

### 5.5 Equipment and Instrument Notes

- Instrument ID (serial number or lab ID)
- Calibration status (when was it last calibrated? did you verify in
  the field?)
- Settings (logging interval, flow rate, method name)
- Any malfunctions, error messages, or anomalies

### 5.6 Deviations from SOPs

If you deviate from the standard procedure for any reason, record:

- What you did differently and why
- Whether the deviation may affect data quality
- Who authorized the deviation (if applicable)

### 5.7 Departure

Before leaving the site, record:

- Time of departure
- Summary of work completed and any work left undone
- Disposition of samples (e.g., "cooler with ice, to lab by 12:00")
- Any follow-up actions needed


## 6. Sketches and Diagrams

A simple sketch is often worth more than a paragraph of text. Include
sketches of:

- Site layout showing sampling locations, landmarks, and compass
  orientation
- Equipment placement (sensor positions, transect layout, plot
  boundaries)
- Anything unusual (erosion features, spill boundaries, wildlife
  sightings relevant to the study)

Label all sketches with a north arrow, approximate scale, date, and
your initials.


## 7. Photographs

### 7.1 When to Photograph

- At the start of every visit: a general site photo showing conditions
- Each sampling location before and after sampling
- Equipment installations and sensor positions
- Anything unusual or noteworthy (damage, contamination indicators,
  unexpected conditions)
- Calibration setups

### 7.2 Photo Naming and Logging

Record in the notebook the photo number (from the camera/phone) and a
brief description for every photo taken:

> "Photo IMG\_4231: Plot BFS-03 looking NE, pre-sampling, 08:22"

Transfer photos to the project folder within 48 hours and rename using
the convention:

`YYYY-MM-DD_SiteID_Description_PhotoNumber.jpg`


## 8. Corrections and Errors

- Never erase, white-out, or obliterate an entry.
- To correct an error, draw a single line through the incorrect text so
  it remains legible, write the correction nearby, and initial and date
  the change.
- If you skip a page or leave blank space, draw a diagonal line through
  the unused area and initial it to prevent later additions.


## 9. Chain of Custody

When samples will be submitted to an analytical laboratory (internal or
external), complete a Chain of Custody (COC) form. The COC must
accompany the samples and include:

- Project name and PI
- Sample IDs matching the field notebook entries
- Date and time of collection
- Number and type of containers
- Analyses requested
- Preservatives applied
- Signatures at each transfer (field to transport, transport to lab)

Record the COC form number in the field notebook for cross-reference.


## 10. Data Transcription

### 10.1 Timeline

Transcribe field data into the project database or spreadsheet within
**48 hours** of returning from the field. Delays increase the risk of
transcription errors and data loss.

### 10.2 Procedure

1. Enter data from the notebook into the standardized project
   spreadsheet or R script.
2. Have a second person verify the transcription against the original
   notebook entries (or perform a self-check against the notebook).
3. Flag any entries that are ambiguous, illegible, or questionable.
   Resolve with the original recorder.
4. Store the digital file per the project's data management plan (see
   [SOP-L802](../lab_sops/SOP-L802-quality-control.qmd), Section 7.2).


## 11. Notebook Archiving

- Completed notebooks are the property of the EA Program and must not
  be taken home or discarded.
- When a notebook is full or a project ends, write the date range on
  the cover and file it in the designated notebook archive (SGM 133,
  labeled shelf).
- Notebooks must be retained for a minimum of 5 years after the end of
  the project, or longer if required by a funding agency.
- If digital scans are desired, photograph or scan every used page and
  store as a PDF in the project archive:
  `data/notebooks/YYYY_ProjectName_NotebookNN.pdf`


## 12. Common Mistakes to Avoid

| Mistake                                  | Why It Matters                           |
|:-----------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Recording data on scrap paper "to copy later" | Scrap paper gets lost; transcription introduces errors |
| Omitting the date or time               | Data cannot be placed in temporal context |
| Omitting GPS coordinates                | Samples cannot be linked to spatial data  |
| Omitting weather conditions             | Weather affects many environmental measurements |
| Writing in pencil                        | Pencil fades and can be erased; use waterproof ink |
| Leaving blank pages without striking through | Creates the appearance that data could be added later |
| Not recording deviations from SOPs      | Unexplained deviations undermine data defensibility |
| Waiting days to transcribe data          | Memory fades; illegible entries cannot be deciphered |

## 15. Training Record

Before conducting independent field work, all personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Demonstrate a properly formatted notebook entry (header block,
   sample records, sketch, photo log) during a supervised field visit
3. Be signed off by the field lead or PI
